title: The pre-speech placebo is significant and at least as large as the speech-day effect, and the defenses against a slow-moving common cause do not close the gap.
summary: The p. 25 text says BR "did not predict" the VIX change in the two days before the speech, but the printed placebo is significant (β = .041, p = .017) and at least as large as the speech-day estimate (0.036, Table 2 Model 2), with a larger t (2.4 against 2.0).
excerpt: did not predict
why_it_matters: A speech cannot move the VIX before it is given, so a significant pre-speech association means something correlated with BR can produce the speech-day coefficient without the speech, and the drafting, pair, prior-VIX and omitted-variable checks do not rule that out.
settle: Report the placebo with the Model 2 controls, estimate daily BR coefficients from t-5 to t+5 and test the leads jointly and against t0, print the prior-VIX estimates, benchmark the pair test against random pairs, report one omitted-variable bound, and correct the p. 25 sentence.

title: The p. 25 control does not separate lost taken-for-grantedness from the reading that backing paragraphs carry news about the policy rules.
summary: Your theory holds that stating the backing lowers its taken-for-grantedness and so widens market judgments.
excerpt: the nature and boundaries of monetary policy objectives and conventional tools
why_it_matters: If backing paragraphs convey news about policy rules or their likely change, or fall at points in the meeting cycle, ordinary asset pricing predicts the H1 sign without any loss of taken-for-grantedness.
settle: Report BR split into restatement and change-discussing shares, show whether BR varies with days to the next FOMC meeting, and add a pre-meeting indicator and its interaction with BR.

title: The outcome is the t-1 to t0 change in U.S. equity implied volatility, but the paper concludes that backing "causes uncertainty in financial markets around the world."
summary: What evidence beyond the speech-day VIX change shows that the policy framework, rather than near-term volatility expectations, became less taken for granted?
excerpt: causes uncertainty in financial markets around the world.
why_it_matters: The VIX change includes risk aversion and does not measure the dispersion of judgments the theory names, so it does not show that the framework became less taken for granted or that uncertainty rose beyond U.S. equities.
settle: Report BR coefficients for t+1, t+3, and t+5, add a dispersion outcome such as professional rate forecasts where aligned data exist, and restate the p. 25 claim at the scope of the test.

title: The paper does not say what BR adds to finance research on Fed speech content, or to Harmon, Green and Goodnight (2015), whose model it tests.
summary: If the paper contributes to central-bank communication, you must show what BR adds to known speech effects.
excerpt: A key insight of this study is that Toulmin’s linguistic concept of backing can be mapped directly onto institutional theorists’ concept of taken-for-granted assumptions.
sources: contrib-closest (Bligh and Hess 2007; Born, Ehrmann and Fratzscher 2011) stage-2/contribution.md
why_it_matters: Uncited work already finds that coded Fed Chair language forecasts market movements and that speech effects concentrate in the crisis, so a reader cannot tell what BR adds to known content effects or to Harmon et al.'s model.
settle: State what BR adds to the Fed-speech findings, present the theory as a test of Harmon et al., and engage the cited central-bank and legitimacy work.

title: BR may capture missing outlook content and speech topic rather than reaffirmation, and the paper does not show that its coding was blind to outcomes.
summary: BR is backing paragraphs over all paragraphs, and p. 22 calls speeches that "discuss the current outlook of the economy" low-BR speeches.
excerpt: discuss the current outlook of the economy
why_it_matters: If BR stands in for the absence of outlook content or for topic, or if coders knew the outcomes, the H1 coefficient can arise without any effect of reaffirmation.
settle: Report BR's R-squared on the other regressors and its within-topic variation, build Model 2 up from BR alone, code outlook paragraphs and add their share beside BR, and compare BR estimates from blind re-coding of a random sample.

title: The standard errors ignore speeches that may share trading days, the sample was trimmed on residuals from an unnamed model, and most robustness checks print no estimates.
summary: The paper reports 40 pairs of speeches within three days of each other, so some may share event-window dates, yet the errors are robust only, and the GEE check links each speech's error to the same Chair's prior speech.
excerpt: robust regressions with robust standard errors
why_it_matters: The main estimate has a one-tailed p of about .023, so unaddressed dependence across shared trading days, trimming on residuals that may come from the outcome, and unreported robustness estimates leave its significance unverified.
settle: Cluster errors by trading date or week, name the trimming model and the estimator, reconcile 337 and 339, report the main models with the seven speeches retained, and add an appendix table of BR under each check.

title: The tone and fear moderators may not measure the emotions H2 and H3 name, and the conditional effects stated in the text are untested and do not match the estimates.
summary: LIWC positive words such as *good* and *favorable* usually describe the economy in Fed speeches, and general dictionaries misclassify financial text (Loughran and McDonald 2011).
excerpt: in fact, reduces
why_it_matters: If tone measures economic content and fear includes the day after the speech and tracks the macro era, the H2 and H3 interactions do not show emotional framing, and the stated conditional effects are untested and larger than the estimates give.
settle: Re-score tone on non-backing paragraphs and with a finance dictionary, rebuild fear from days before t0, add BR x word count and BR x existing uncertainty, and report conditional effects with standard errors or narrow the claims.

title: The crisis extension, called "additional validation" in the Discussion, comes from a subsample selected on both moderators and a model with more parameters than speeches.
summary: The Results call this analysis tentative and "preliminary evidence", but the Discussion calls it "additional validation".
excerpt: additional validation
why_it_matters: The crisis estimate matches the full-sample estimate, the interaction p-values match unstated one-tailed tests, and the 48-speech reversal uses a 58-df model on 48 speeches cut on a post-outcome moderator, so the scope condition is not shown.
settle: Report Models 2 and 5 for crisis and non-crisis speeches with N and tails, say which terms were kept for the 48 speeches, show other cutoffs, estimate the same cell outside the crisis, or describe the result as preliminary.

title: The paper does not say how speeches on weekends or late in the trading day were mapped to the event window.
summary: The paper does not say how speeches on weekends or late in the trading day were mapped to the t-1 to t0 window.
excerpt: Consistent with work in finance (Chang, Pinegar, and Ravichandran, 1993; Dubois and Louvet, 1996; Choudhry, 2000; Connolly, Stivers, and Sun, 2005), I controlled for day on which the speech took place by creating dummy variables for each weekday.
why_it_matters: A speech dated to the wrong trading day pairs its BR with a VIX change it could not have caused, and if delivery time varies with audience the error may be related to BR.
settle: State the mapping rule and delivery times, and re-estimate without weekend and late-day speeches.

title: Thessaly (2008), the source for the mediator step, could not be found.
summary: The only source you cite for the step from lower taken-for-grantedness to more dispersed judgments, the 2008 Organization Science article listed under Thessaly in your references, could not be found, and its stated pages overlap another article in that volume.
excerpt: Thus, diminishing the market’s taken-for-grantedness of these assumptions will reduce market participants’ ability to rely on “the way one always does things” to make forecasts about the future, producing greater heterogeneity in overall judgments and decisions made in the market (Thessaly, 2008).
why_it_matters: The step from lost taken-for-grantedness to dispersed judgments has no locatable support.
settle: Correct or replace the citation.

title: Brandvold and Halvorsen (2011), the source for central bankers' beliefs, could not be found.
summary: The only scholarly source you cite for central bankers' beliefs, the 2011 Journal of Monetary Economics article listed under Brandvold and Halvorsen in your references, could not be found, and the pages it gives belong to other articles.
excerpt: This empirical setting is particularly noteworthy because the argument I am proposing runs counter to the prevailing wisdom of central bankers (Brandvold and Halvorsen, 2011).
why_it_matters: The prevailing view the paper argues against has no locatable scholarly source.
settle: Correct or replace the citation.

title: The relative claim on p. 7 and the absolute claim on p. 8 about backing going without saying do not fit together.
summary: Page 7 says the backing is only more taken for granted than the other components, but p. 8 says it "typically goes without saying"; say how backing the Chair discusses regularly can still lose taken-for-grantedness.
excerpt: typically goes without saying
why_it_matters: H1 needs backing that is taken for granted, yet the Chair states it regularly.
settle: Explain how routinely stated backing can still lose taken-for-grantedness when stated.

title: The word-count coefficient cannot be read as printed.
summary: The word-count coefficient prints as -0.000 (0.000) in every model, so the Discussion's claim that longer speeches reduce uncertainty cannot be checked; report it per 1,000 words.
excerpt: Specifically, Table 2 indicates that longer speeches significantly reduce market uncertainty.
why_it_matters: A Discussion claim cannot be checked against the table.
settle: Rescale word count to thousands of words.

title: The two practical recommendations point in opposite directions.
summary: Which recommendation, wrapping backing in positive language or discussing the assumptions more regularly, does the evidence support, and what result would show that the extra uncertainty deters risk-taking?
excerpt: Perhaps our institutional leaders should discuss these taken-for-granted assumptions more regularly.
why_it_matters: The practical implications do not follow clearly from the results.
settle: Say which recommendation the evidence supports.

title: Business media fear in Model 4 carries stars its standard error cannot support.
summary: Business media fear in Model 4 is 0.005** with a standard error of 2.924, which cannot be significant.
excerpt: Significance tests are one-tailed for directional hypotheses, two-tailed for control variables.
why_it_matters: A table entry is internally impossible.
settle: Correct the Model 4 entry.

title: The Model 5 adjusted R-squared does not follow from its R-squared.
summary: The Model 5 adjusted R-squared of 0.261 does not follow from its R-squared of 0.355 with 339 observations and 60 df, which give 0.216.
excerpt: All models include year, topic, and local audience fixed-effects.
why_it_matters: A fit statistic is inconsistent with the table.
settle: Correct the Model 5 adjusted R-squared.

title: Text-only estimates label their uncertainty as a variance.
summary: The text-only estimates label their uncertainty "σ2," which reads as a variance, not a standard error.
excerpt: σ2
why_it_matters: Readers cannot check the reported p-values.
settle: Label the standard errors as such.

title: Stars on the positive-tone main effect fit one-tailed tests only.
summary: The stars on the positive-tone main effect require one-tailed tests, but the Table 2 note says controls are tested two-tailed.
excerpt: Significance tests are one-tailed for directional hypotheses, two-tailed for control variables.
why_it_matters: The stars do not follow the stated testing convention.
settle: Apply the stated convention or state the test used.

title: Audience fixed effects do not address attention within audience categories.
summary: Audience fixed effects remove five category means, not attention differences within a category; a t0 newswire count per speech and its interaction with BR would address this.
excerpt: All models include year, topic, and local audience fixed-effects.
why_it_matters: Attention to a speech could explain both its content and the market response.
settle: Add a t0 newswire count and its interaction with BR.

title: The paper does not say which traders hold the framework as taken for granted.
summary: Under your mechanism, should traders who follow Fed policy closely react more or less to backing than others, and can you show which group moves the VIX on high-BR days?
excerpt: This relationship is likely due to the fact that higher levels of sophistication are potentially required to understand the complexities and implications of the assumptions underlying the Fed’s monetary policy framework.
why_it_matters: The mechanism does not say whose taken-for-grantedness changes.
settle: State the prediction by trader type and test it if possible.

title: No BR x Chair term tests whether markets read backing differently across Chairs.
summary: Year fixed effects nearly absorb Chair identity, but no BR x Chair term tests whether markets read backing differently across three Chairs with very different speech counts.
excerpt: The final sample thus consisted of 337 speeches (159 by Alan Greenspan, 166 by Ben Bernanke, and 12 by Janet Yellen) (see Figure 2).
why_it_matters: The BR slope may differ by Chair.
settle: Add a BR x Chair interaction.

title: The VIX measures the size of expected moves, not their direction.
summary: The paper describes the VIX as traders' estimate of the direction of the S&P 500, but it measures the expected size of moves, so the argument about optimistic and pessimistic directions is not tested by it.
excerpt: The VIX thus represents options traders’ estimates of the direction of the S&P 500 over the next month by providing an aggregate measure of the variance of option prices on any given day.
why_it_matters: The outcome does not measure what the emotion argument predicts.
settle: Describe the VIX correctly and align the argument with it.

title: The framing does not name the view it overturns, and the promised reversal is recast as complementary.
summary: The introduction says we still know little about leaders who reaffirm assumptions and uses a practitioner belief as its foil, while signaling theory, which holds the view the paper argues against, appears only in the Discussion, where the promised reversal becomes complementary under a condition never measured.
excerpt: My primary finding also appears to be somewhat at odds with signaling theory (Akerlof, 1970; Spence, 1973), which is arguably the most dominant theory for understanding how communication influences financial markets (Tetlock, 2007; Graffin, Carpenter, and Boivie, 2011).
why_it_matters: The introduction does not say what existing theory gets wrong, and the Discussion softens the claimed reversal.
settle: Name signaling theory as the foil in the introduction and keep the claim consistent across sections.

title: The Fedspeak controls come from dictionaries validated elsewhere.
summary: The three language controls for Fedspeak come from dictionaries validated in other domains, and the partial vagueness dictionary is not specified.
excerpt: I controlled for speech complexity by using the Flesch-Kincaid reading grade level (Kincaid et al., 1975); speech abstractness by using a word dictionary compiled and validated by Mergenthaler (1996); and speech vagueness by using a partial dictionary compiled and validated by Hiller and colleagues (1969).
why_it_matters: The controls may not capture Fedspeak.
settle: Specify the vagueness dictionary and justify the measures for Fed text.

title: The interactions assume a linear change in the backing-ratio slope.
summary: Both interactions use a single linear product term, with no binned check that the BR slope changes linearly with tone or fear.
excerpt: Model 3 adds the first interaction term between the BR and speech positive tone.
why_it_matters: The moderation results assume a functional form that is not checked.
settle: Add a binned estimator check.

title: The moderator hypotheses add an incremental contribution.
summary: H2 and H3 extend Pfarrer et al. (2010), as the paper says, so their space might go to the H1 mechanism.
excerpt: However, my findings extend their work in at least two important ways.
why_it_matters: Space on the moderators could go to the main mechanism.
settle: Treat the moderators as secondary analyses.

title: Ease-of-retrieval research offers a testable micro-mechanism.
summary: Research on ease of retrieval in persuasion offers a tested micro-mechanism for H1 and a moderator, audience elaboration, that the paper could use or rule out.
excerpt: Recall that Hypothesis 1 contends that when the Fed Chair begins to reaffirm the backing explicitly, this will prompt market participants to think of alternatives to the current way of doing things and lead them to make decisions in increasingly diverging directions.
why_it_matters: An existing micro-mechanism could sharpen H1.
settle: Use or rule out the ease-of-retrieval account.

title: The VXX translation does not follow from the coefficient.
summary: The VXX translation does not follow from a spot-VIX coefficient, because the VXX began trading in 2009 and its issuer states it will not necessarily track the VIX.
excerpt: A $10,000 investment would hypothetically gross a one-day return of $100 (1 percent).
why_it_matters: The stated practical size is not supported.
settle: Drop or correct the VXX translation.

title: Table 1 prints an impossible SD for the location dummy and a rounded-to-zero SD for fear.
summary: Table 1 prints an SD of 0.64 for the Washington, D.C. dummy, impossible for a 0/1 variable with mean 0.29, and prints fear's SD as 0.00; report it unrounded.
excerpt: I created a dummy variable for the speech location by assigning a “1” to speeches given in Washington, D.C., which is the Fed’s headquarters and the meeting location of the FOMC.
why_it_matters: Descriptive statistics cannot be checked or used to scale effects.
settle: Correct the location SD and print fear's SD unrounded.

title: Loughran and McDonald (2011) is misspelled.
summary: The reference list misspells McDonald as "McDonaold" in Loughran and McDonald (2011).
excerpt: McDonaold
why_it_matters: A citation error.
settle: Correct the spelling.

title: The audience correlations do not validate BR as a measure of reaffirmation.
summary: The audience correlations show that BR varies with audience, not that it measures reaffirmation rather than technical content, and the benchmark is the expectation of the author of about half the speeches; check BR against an independent coding of restatement.
excerpt: Equally important is that this also provides strong support for the construct and measurement validity of the BR, since it confirms the expectation of Bernanke, the author of many of the speeches in my sample.
why_it_matters: The validity claim for BR depends on a correlation that technical content would also produce.
settle: Correlate BR with an independent coding of whether paragraphs restate the framework.
